extracted.intended_audience: writers or students seeking criteria for depicting the 'true philosopher' (readers of Plato / characterizers of philosophical types)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards and descriptive criteria for the 'true philosopher' (vs. lovers of opinion/imitators) — useful for writers building philosopher characters or students analyzing Platonic character-types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lover of the vision of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers are 'lovers of the vision of truth' — those who pursue the sight of absolute/eternal truth rather than mere appearances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish this from mere lovers of sights and sounds: the philosopher recognises absolute beauty (the Idea) and can separate the Idea from the particular objects which participate in it. Antipattern: conflating appreciation of beautiful particulars with genuine philosophical insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to apprehend absolute beauty / Forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Able to attain the sight of absolute beauty and distinguish the Idea from participating objects, not putting copies in place of the real object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few attain this; those who can follow a guide to the idea of beauty are 'wide awake' (true knowers). Example contrast: the dreamer who mistakes copies for originals. For characterization, show ability to perceive essences rather than only particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge versus opinion (distinct faculties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge corresponds to pure being and is infallible; opinion occupies an intermediate faculty concerned with things that are partly being and partly not-being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical characters should operate from knowledge (being) rather than opinion (the flux). Use the idea of an intermediate class (opinion) to portray characters who are sensible but not true knowers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness / hatred of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: The true philosopher must 'love the truth' and never intentionally receive falsehood; cannot be a lover of falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray philosophers as having an aversion to deceit and self-deception. Antipattern: a philosopher who values rhetoric over truth or knowingly accepts falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in learning / love of study
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers must take pleasure in learning; those who find study painful or make little progress will not be genuine philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show sustained devotion to intellectual toil and intrinsic enjoyment of inquiry, not careerism or showy scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good memory / retention
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosopher should have a good memory; forgetfulness yields an 'empty vessel' and frustrates philosophical study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing, give philosopher characters reliable recollection and cumulative learning; avoid depicting them as chronically forgetful if you intend them as true philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quickness to learn / intellectual aptitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Quickness and facility in learning are among the natural gifts of the true philosopher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate rapid comprehension, ease with abstract patterns, and quick assimilation of instruction as markers of philosophical potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance / diminished bodily pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: The true philosopher is absorbed in pleasures of the soul and 'will hardly feel bodily pleasure'—temperate and not covetous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict restraint regarding material and sensual desires; antipattern: a philosopher primarily motivated by wealth, status, or bodily indulgence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-covetousness / not motivated by possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers are the 'reverse of covetous'; motives that make others desirous of having and spending are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize them as uninterested in material accumulation and transactional gain; their aims are intellectual and civic rather than personal enrichment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence of mind / absence of meanness
rubrics_metrics.description: No secret corner of illiberality; meanness is antagonistic to a soul longing after the whole of things — philosophers possess grandeur of soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray magnanimity, generosity of spirit, and refusal to be petty. Antipattern: petty, small-minded thinking presented as philosophical greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage / not fearful (including fearlessness of death)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers are courageous; the lover of the true being will not account death fearful and is not cowardly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show willingness to face danger or death for truth or duty. Courage here ties to moral steadfastness as well as physical bravery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice, gentleness, and sociability
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosopher should be just and gentle, not rude or unsociable; these signs can distinguish the philosophical nature even in youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include social virtues — fairness, kindness, and cooperative temper — as part of a philosophical character's profile; avoid isolating them as misanthropes by default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion / harmonious constitution of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is akin to proportion; philosophers have a naturally well-proportioned and gracious mind that moves toward true being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey inner balance, moderation, and aesthetic harmony of character. Antipattern: disproportionate minds that are brilliant but sorely unbalanced in virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on being rather than multiplicity (pursuit of essences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lover of knowledge strives after being (essences) and will not rest in the multiplicity of individuals; he moves toward knowledge of true nature of every essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict philosophical concern for general principles and essences rather than mere particulars or sensational details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to popular opinion / not pandering to the mob
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher will not be induced to believe in the many-beautiful (public opinion) rather than absolute beauty; the world (mob) will censure philosophers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show tension between philosopher characters and popular tastes; they should avoid catering to applause and be immune (ideally) to mass approbation. Antipattern: philosophers who simply seek mass approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability to corruption by environment / need for proper nurture
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest natures are especially sensitive to alien conditions and may become corrupt or 'the most noxious of all weeds' if ill-educated or badly placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a philosopher character goes wrong, attribute it plausibly to bad education, corrupt society, or brittle environment rather than to an inherent lack of ability. Useful for plotting fall-from-grace arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from imitators / not merely lovers of sounds and sights
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitators (lovers of opinion) are fond of tones, colours, and artifice but lack sight of absolute beauty; philosophers are distinct from these sham followers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When contrasting characters, mark imitators by superficial tastes, eagerness for popular praise, and inability to follow guides to deeper truth; show philosophers as seeking underlying realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability to rule: guardians must have knowledge of true being
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who grasp eternal and unchangeable truths are best qualified to guard laws and institutions and therefore should be rulers (guardians) of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For narratives about governance or leadership, justify philosopher-rulers by their capacity to see common good and eternal principles; conversely, depict failure when rulers lack such insight.
